Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ is located on the southern side of Patan Darbar Square. Unlike other bāhāḥs, Haugaḥ has no affiliation with Śākyas or Vajrācāryas. Rather, it is a private Bāhāḥ belonging to the Rājakarṇikāra community. The Bāhāḥ can be accessed via the carved door located at the east wing of the monastic complex. The entry porch of the complex has four wooden pillars and is suggestive of a colonnaded phalcā with seating space added at a later date. The courtyard measures 10.0m x 9.8m and is encircled by a plinth with a depth of 1.1m. The sunken courtyard is 42cm deep and contains a dharmadhātu maṇḍala and an aśoka caitya. The sanctum building faces east and has a central main door with two stone lions guarding the steps that lead up to it. The door is surmounted by a wooden toraṇa that exhibits three eight-handed tantric deities. The façade has a tikijhyāḥ on its first floor and a trikhājhyā on the second floor.

The three-storied esoteric building faces east and has a phujā above it. Four decorative struts support the sloping roof, which is clad in brass. The lower roof is covered with corrugated metal sheets and supported by six struts. Four of these display images of gods whilst the other two are decorated with flower motifs. The façade of the second floor has a carved window. Glass panes have been fixed in the window frame, and it is flanked by two tikijhyās. The first floor houses the āgama of the Bāhāḥ, and this floor also has a brass-clad trikhājhyāḥ. A brass-clad aedicule has been fixed to the right of the window and a gilded window has been installed to its left. Above the middle window, one can see a wall painting of seven tathāgatas. The sanctum of the Bāhāḥ is on the ground floor. A brass toraṇa exhibiting images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara surmounts the brass-clad entrance of the sanctum. The door is flanked by concrete images of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. An image of Mahākāla can be found to the right of this door, whilst images of Sarasvatī and Hanumān are located to its left, alongside an empty niche that represents the main deity of the āgama. Two stone lions, metal flags and hanging bells have been placed on either side of the entrance. The statue of the main deity of the Bāhāḥ, Akṣobhya, is made of stone and is adorned in lhegā.

The building attached to the dyaḥchẽ to the north is used by the Sanāḥ Guṭhī, which is also called Rājakarṇikāra (Halvāī) Śaraṇa Guṭhī. The southern building attached to the sanctum belongs to the Bāhāḥ. A Buddha-statue can be found sleeping on the first floor of this house. The room is named after this statue and is known as 'Relaxing Buddha'. A pañcāvaliyukta caitya and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala have also been placed inside the room. This room is used as an office by the Rājakarṇikāra society.

No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide any information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ. During the Malla period, elephants were reared at the Haugala Ṭola. This area was therefore once known as Hastināgala. The word 'Hastināgala' gradually morphed into variations such as Hātigala, Hatigla, Haugala and Haugaḥ. At that time, one of the ministers of the Malla Kings suggested he bring two Brahmins from Kannauj, India to prepare sweets for him. The king invited these two individuals and offered them land at Hastināgala Ṭola. The Brahmins were called Rājakarṇikāra. They later became integrated into the Buddhist Newar community and established their own bāhāḥ. Later, King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha allowed them to open a sweet shop near the shrine of Nārāyaṇa at the present Nārāyaṇahiṭī compound (cf. Locke 1985, 229). A dense population of Karṇikāra caste members surrounds the Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ.

Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ is located to the west of Uku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). It is located inside an L-shaped courtyard which can be accessed through a narrow underpass by a six storied building. The bāhāḥ is on the way to Thāpāhiṭī from Mahābuddha. The main monument building is a small structure attached to a residential building to the west. It is not visible from the main entrance; one must walk to the end of the long courtyard and turn right to find an adjacent courtyard. Together, they form an open L-shaped space. Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Oku Bāhāh.

The god house sits on a stone plinth raised above the ground. The main sanctum is constructed from timber and exhibits intricately carved door jambs and a toraṇa thā (the place for toraṇa). Four corner posts have been carved to resemble the column that supports the three-tiered roofs, which in turn are covered with brass plates. The structure's pinnacle is missing. Behind the monument, there is a four-storey residential building with a projecting carved open window at the center flanked by two vertical lattice windows on either sides on the first floor. Above this, the second floor boasts a central and elaborately carved triple-opening window. The ground floor has a three-bayed colonnaded structure, and the central bay is occupied by this monument. In front of the monument, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya (2 m high) and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala (65 cm high) on a raised platform paved in stone.

The structure of this bāhāḥ differs from other bāhāḥ of Patan; this bāhāḥ has no kvāḥpāḥchẽ. The brass-clad roof of the temple is supported by struts that display images of Lokeśvaras. Previously, one could find an image of Amitābha inside the temple's sanctum, but this is presently at the home of one of the main authorities of the bāhāḥ. A toraṇa above the entrance of the sanctum shows Lokeśvara with Prajñāpāramitā to her right and another Lokeśvara to her left. Śākya (1994, 118-119) writes that the sanctum also contained wall paintings of Māyādevī, Cintāmaṇi Lokeśvara, Padmasaṃbhava, Harihariharivāhanalokeśvara, Uṣṇīṣavijaya, Āryatārā, Dhvajāgrakeyūrī and the first Bhīmarathārohaṇa. However, only three of them (Uṣṇīṣavijaya, Āryatārā and Padmasaṃbhava) are still there.

Bhājudhana Śākya was a member of the saṅgha of Oku Bāhāḥ and he established this bāhāḥ with help of his elder brother Bhīmarāja and other family members. Bhājudhana had shop in Tibet where he sold gold jewellery. He established this vihāra using the money he earned from his business. As a result, this vihāra is also called Hiraṇyalābha Vihāra. In NS 1027 (1907 CE), Bhājudhana established a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya in the courtyard. Two years later, he made a small god house and enshrined the image of Akṣobhya inside it.

This Bāhāḥ is located in Khācheñ Ṭola between Naka Bahī and Dhalāyacā Ṭola and is a branch of the Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra. The stone-paved residential courtyard measures only 3 m x 3.2 m and can be accessed from the north, through an alley underneath a house connecting the courtyard with the Swotha street. The courtyard has a unique caitya at its center. It is one of a kind in Patan since its garbhagṛha, harmikā, trayodaśabhuvana and pinnacle are all made of crystal.

To the east of the Caitya, is a traditional door which still remains within the modern house fabric. The special carved timber door (missing the threshold) with an extended lintel must have been an entry to a special place related to the rituals but at present, the space is rented for commercial use.

The shrine of the main deity of the Bāhāḥ is lost, and a space to the west is still empty waiting for the deity, an east-facing Akṣobhya Buddha, to return from the guthi member who took it to his home when the adjacent house was demolished.

An inscription informs that Jayānanda built the Caitya in 1801 CE (NS 921). According to local informants, Jayānanda Śākya was a professional sculptor who used to make images of crystal. This crystal Caitya sits on a copper pedestal, which is shaped as a lotus with three folds of petals turned upwards. This lotus sits on a slim base that gently increases in circumference as it nears the ground. Beneath this is a double-tier rectangular stone plinth. The caitya is framed by a five-tier copper pinnacle, which is supported by four copper serpents, with their tails near the top and their heads facing downwards. It is encased in a metal cage and has a brass roof. Above the pinnacle is an unbrella (chatra) with five layers and which is supported by stylised snakes (nāga). There are four images in the four corners of the Caitya . In the southwest corner is an image of the donor (Jayānanda), and in the southeast corner is an image of Garuḍa. Similarly, in the northwest corner there is an image of an elephant, and in the northeast corner there is an image of a lion.

Kapileśvara Mahādeva Mandira is located adjacent to the Bicche Bāhāḥ, Kathmandu. It faces west. The current stone pinnacle of the temple was installed after the previous golden one was stolen. A stone toraṇa featuring chepu adorns the entrance of the sanctum.

A Śivaliṅga is consecrated in the sanctum, and there is also an additional Śivaliṅga inside the sanctum area, its jalaharī faces east.

The inscription installed to the north of the sanctum entrance informs us that it was constructed by Kaṃpālidāsa (Kapiladāsa) and his wife Māneśvarī in 1690 CE (NS 810). The inscription does not mention the caste of Kaṃpālidāsa, but local residents believe that he was from a Pradhāna caste. His family also constructed the Bicche Phalcā (KAT0941) which is adjacent to the temple.

Kaṃpilādāsa’s family endowed land to the temple and established a guṭhī to finance the daily, annual, occasional, and other rituals. However, no official ritual activities take place in the temple in the present-day. Local community members visit the temple and worship the Śivaliṅga in early mornings.

A fire oblation is performed on the day of Śrīpañcamī (Sarasvatīpūjā) in the adjacent Bicche Phalcā (KAT0941). Its guṭhī members also perform a special worship in this temple on that day. Reṇukā Vajrācārya, a member of the local community, has been voluntarily cleaning the temple every Tuesday.

Bhūkampa Smāraka is a stone pillar that stands at the northern end of the Patan Darbar Square and in front of the three-tiered Bhīmasena temple (LAL1380). The stone pillar is based on a double plinth of stone, which is surrounded by a square stone paving measuring 260 cm x 260 cm. The bottom plinth (17 cm high) measures 153 cm x 153 cm whilst the top plinth (25 cm high) measures 97 cm x 97 cm. The pillar is 168 cm high and has a 40 cm square base. The pillar is tapers at the base around a height of 70 cm; above this, it is straight. The top of the pillar has small recessed motifs and has a lotus base for an image of Annapūrṇā (58 cm tall).

This pillar was erected in 1941 by the people of Lalitpur in memory of the devastating 1934 earthquake and in honor of Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera and his assistance. A similar kind of memorial was also established in the Bhugol Park of New Road, Kathmandu. The Patan Darbar Square pillar has an image of Annapūrṇā at its top. Standing upon a lotus pedestal, the goddess is holding a brahmadaṇḍa in her right hand and a water vessel in her left hand. She is wearing a crown and a long garland. Inscriptions have been written on the south and west faces of the pillar. One of these inscriptions records the destruction caused by the earthquake and the progress of the recovery work. In addition to this, it also details some of the development works undertaken by Juddha Śamśera. The inscription states that many people were helped by Juddha Śamśera, who donated 1 million 74 thousand and 913 rupees. It also records the amount of money collected in the assistance fund and its expenditure.

The Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya is located at Kotā Ṭola to the north of Dey Pukhu. Its vedikā stands on a rectangular platform. Above the vedikā one can see a lion throne that displays sculpted images of four lion figures and Caturmahārājas on the four corners and at each of the cardinal directions, respectively. The Four Buddhas have been placed on a throne located on the upward opening single-layer lotus blossoms. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi are located on the eastern, southern, western and northern faces of the caitya respectively. Akṣobhya’s seat is decorated with images of two elephants and Maitreya. Similarly, the south side shows two horses and Vajrapāṇi, the west side displays peacocks and Padmapāṇi, and the north side contains images of Garuḍas and Mañjuśrī. Three layers of lotus petals can be found above the Buddha statues and small statues of the Four Buddhas and Four Tārās are placed above these petals. Cement plaster has been used to join the caitya's garbha and harmikā. The yaḥsĩ has also been plastered with cement.

The structure of the caitya suggests that it can be dated back to the 19-20th century. According to the local residents, it was built by a Tulādhara family. Remnants of a collapsed phalcā lie to the north of the caitya. Local residents assume that a stone inscription is buried somewhere in this rubble.

The structure of the caitya suggests that it can be dated back to the 19-20th century. According to the local residents, it was built by a Tulādhara family. Remnants of a collapsed phalcā lie to the north of the caitya. Local residents assume that a stone inscription is buried somewhere in this rubble.

Baku Nani is one of the courtyards within the Itum Bāhāḥ Ṭola. It is located to the south of Itum Bāhāḥ (KAT1220). Local community members believe that it is named after the fact that the Nani is located at the lower part of the extended Itum Bāhāḥ courtyard.

There is a shrine in the middle of the Nani. A caitya is consecrated inside it, which is the only heritage property in the Nani. Similar caitya examples are also present elsewhere in front of the Itum Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, in Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, and in Kāyegu Nani.

There is no evidence to appoint the initial construction of this caitya. In an inscription inside the sanctum from 1853 CE (NS 973), it is mentioned that the caitya was renovated. In the inscription, the caitya is referred to as Vajradhātu Caitya.

Both Pruscha (1975, 44) and Locke (1985, 290) mention that the temple was constructed in a traditional way and tiled with jhĩgaṭī bricks. However, the temple's entire structure transformed into a cemented construction when it was renovated in 1987 CE.

A Śākya family residing in the nani takes care of the temple and performs daily worship. Previously, on certain days every month, devotees gathered around the temple to recite mantras and other religious texts. This tradition takes place in the present-day twice a year on the full moon day of Kārttika and during the Kathmandu Pañcadāna Festival. On the full moon day of Kārttika, the local residents display various images made of fried pulses and grains. This tradition also continues to this day.

_source.displaydescription:
Measuring 367 x 367 cm in size, the west-facing Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is located in the Bhelāchẽ Tol, to the north of the Durbar Square of Patan. Ṭīkā Bhairava is also known as Unmatta Bhairava or Mahā Bhairava. The Bhelāchẽ Tol was named after this temple; its name derives from the Nevārī word bhelā, meaning Bhairava, and 'hẽ, meaning house.

The main entry gate to the temple is to the west and is flanked by two guardian lions, which in turn have two metal flags between them. In front of the main entry, one can find a brick-paved space that contains several small objects. One of these is a stone Padmapatra, sitting almost at the centre and in line with the main entrance. One can also find a stone trough of an abandoned jarḥũhiti, which measures 50 cm in width and 173 cm in length. The lower banner on its right-hand side is broken.

The Ṭīkā Bhairava temple is a three-storey pagoda-style temple, and stands on a low stone base. All three roofs of the temple are made of copper sheets. Above the entrance is a garuḍa toraṇa showing an image of Bhairava with eight hands. Bhairava is holding gajacarma, ḍamaru, katṛ and kapāla with his right hands, and gajacarma, khaṭvāṅga and naramuṇḍa with his left. The last hand is in a bindu position. Bhairava is at the centre of the toraṇa and is flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra. Behind the toraṇa is a window with a wall painting of Khyā on its left and an image of Kavã on its right. Below the second roof, in front of the window on the western side, one can find a wooden toraṇa with images of similar deities painted in different colors. At the top of the temple is a pinnacle with serpents in its four corners. A banner hangs down from the pinnacle to the bottom of the temple's first roof on the western side.

The sanctum is a colonnaded space with 12 octagonal columns standing in three bays on each side. The central area within this space is demarcated by a 2.1m long wall of 70 cm thickness and two timber posts. Together, these form a square space; the main image of the deity, which faces to the west, is attached to the wall. However, the sanctum does not contain a stone image of the main deity. Instead, there is a metal śivaliṅga, with an image of Bhairava painted on the wall behind it. To the left of the śivaliṅga is a stone image of Gaṇeśa with four arms, and to its right hand side is a stone image of Kumāra, also with four arms.

Uutside, the temple has twenty struts supporing the lowest roof. The four corner struts contain images of śārdūla, while the other 16 struts display images of the Eight Mātṛkās and Eight Bhairavas. Alongside this, the struts to the west also contain images of Rudra Bhairava mounted on a human being, Māheśvarī, Unmatta Bhairava mounted on a lion, and Brahmāyaṇī. The southern struts display Bhairava mounted on a human being, Mahālakṣmī, a Bhairava riding on a horse, and Cāmuṇḍā. To the east, the struts contain images of Bhairava mounted on a bull, Indrāyaṇī, Kapāla Bhairava riding on a snake, and Vārāhī. Finally, the northern struts display images of Bhairava mounted on a Garuḍa, Vaiṣṇavī, Pracaṇḍa Bhairava mounted on a boar, and Kumārī (Tachikawa 2004,17-19).

In the temple area are a bell, a jarũhiṭī, a small stone image of Basāhā and an aniconic stone image of Ajimā. 

According to Pruscha (1975, 176) this temple was built in 1541 but no inscription could be found  to provide evidence of this date. Mention of this temple is, however, made in Kīrtipatākā, a text composed by Kunu Śarmā. It describes images of gods drawn on the walls of the temple (see in Naraharinātha 1961, 12).
